title: What is the Temple?
summary: The Bible presents the temple as a place associated with God’s presence, Israel’s worship, and ordered access. The cited passages show these ideas taking different forms: Solomon’s dedication, a worshiper’s longing in Psalm 84, Jesus’ temple saying in John 2, Hebrews’ discussion of sanctuary service, and Revelation’s vision of a city with no separate temple.
historical_context: The references here depict Solomon dedicating a temple in 1 Kings 8 and later biblical writers reflecting on the temple’s meaning. They do not provide a full chronology of Jerusalem’s successive temples or archaeological evidence for their construction and destruction. The temple should therefore be understood here through the cited texts, not as a complete historical reconstruction.
canonical_context: Exodus 25:8–9 describes the sanctuary as a place for God to dwell among Israel, while 1 Kings 8 holds that promise together with Solomon’s acknowledgment that even the highest heaven cannot contain God. Psalm 84 gives voice to longing for the temple courts. In John 2, Jesus speaks of the temple of his body; Hebrews 9 discusses sanctuary service; Revelation 21 pictures God and the Lamb as the city’s temple. These are related texts, but each makes its point in a different genre and setting.
later_christian_reception: John 2:13–22 connects Jesus’ temple saying with his body, and Hebrews 9 interprets sanctuary service within its argument about Jesus’ priestly ministry. Revelation 21:22–27 presents the renewed city without a separate temple because God and the Lamb are its temple. These passages develop temple language in distinct ways; they do not make every earlier temple passage say the same thing.
literary_context: The references move across different kinds of writing: Exodus gives sanctuary instructions, 1 Kings narrates a royal dedication and prayer, Psalm 84 is a song of longing, John narrates a dispute over Jesus’ saying, Hebrews reasons from sanctuary service, and Revelation describes a vision of the renewed city. Keeping those forms in view helps explain why the temple can be a physical place in one passage and an image used in a later argument or vision in another.
covenantal_significance: In Exodus 25:8–9, the sanctuary is made so God may dwell among Israel. At the dedication in 1 Kings 8, the cloud fills the house, yet Solomon also says the heavens cannot contain God. The pairing presents divine nearness without treating the temple as a container for God. Later texts draw on temple language in their own settings, especially John 2, Hebrews 9, and Revelation 21.
canonical_role: What is the Temple? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: The cited passages associate the temple with presence, worship, and ordered sanctuary service, but they do not reduce its meaning to one formula such as ‘atonement.’ Notice what each text emphasizes: dedication and prayer in 1 Kings 8, longing in Psalm 84, sanctuary service in Hebrews 9, and God’s presence throughout the city in Revelation 21.

John 2 links Jesus’ temple saying with his body, Hebrews 9 uses sanctuary service in an argument about Jesus’ priestly ministry, and Revelation 21 depicts the whole city as having no separate temple. These are distinct New Testament uses; they should not be flattened into a single claim that the temple simply ‘becomes’ one thing.
